claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt particles.
The initial nanoparticles are likely a disordered FCC solid solution.
Below 10 nm, high surface-to-volume ratio and surface-energy minimization cause the sluggish-diffusion assumption to break down.
Au has the lowest surface energy among the constituent elements and therefore rapidly segregates to the nanoparticle surface.
Au has the highest vapor pressure among the constituent elements.
The surface-energy driving force scales inversely with particle radius.
For radii below 10 nm, the surface-energy driving force becomes large enough to overcome sluggish-diffusion barriers.
The Gibbs-Thomson or Kelvin effect enhances evaporation from the smallest particles.
Evaporation and dissolution into larger particles cause rapid loss of particles smaller than 5 nm.
Ostwald ripening causes smaller particles to disappear while feeding larger particles.
Heating produces an Au-rich shell on the surviving particles.
Particles facet or spheroidize during heating to reduce surface energy or total surface area.
No bulk separation into distinct intermetallic phases occurs in the particle cores within the heating timeframe.
For particles larger than 50 nm, bulk sluggish diffusion may dominate and behavior may resemble bulk high-entropy-alloy predictions.
The proposed mechanism requires vacuum, whereas oxidation would dominate in air.
Cu has a higher vapor pressure than Au and may compete with Au in evaporation.
An inert-gas control would suppress evaporation relative to the vacuum experiment.
Retention of equiatomic composition and spherical shape without significant size loss up to 1000 K would falsify the proposed surface-driven mechanism.
Observation of bulk Co-rich or Ni-rich phase separation instead of surface segregation would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism identify Au as the constituent with the highest vapor pressure, while the uncertainty field states that Cu has a higher vapor pressure than Au.
